rows.bounded_proposition: For the Middle Kingdom, specialist Egyptology distinguishes free lower-status people, servants, conscripts and fugitives from enslavement; foreign prisoners could be explicitly enslaved. The reviewed packet therefore supports a bounded claim of slavery through foreign-prisoner enslavement around the Middle Kingdom, while other dependent labour categories remain distinct.
rows.required_abstention: Do not translate every hm/bak servant, conscript, dependent worker or coerced labourer into a slave, and do not infer a widespread hereditary chattel-slavery system or prevalence level from this evidence.
rows.temporal_applicability: Middle Kingdom context c.2100–1700 BCE; applicable to the 2000 BCE anchor at period level, not an exact dated event.
rows.temporal_precision: broad historical period; category distinctions are period-level
rows.evidence_locus: Middle Kingdom Egyptian documentary/literary and institutional context
rows.inference_extent: Middle Kingdom Egypt only at the level supported by specialist synthesis; no numeric or universal prevalence inference
rows.law_practice_note: The packet distinguishes statuses and enslavement categories; it does not quantify legal uniformity or compliance.
rows.language_access_limitations: English-accessible specialist synthesis reviewed; underlying Egyptian terminology is mediated through Egyptological interpretation rather than independently retranslated here.

sources.title: Slavery in Pharaonic and Hellenistic Egypt
sources.author: Antonio Loprieno
sources.notes: Directly distinguishes nḏs, ḥm/bȝk, ḥsb and tšj and limits 'true slavery' in this period to foreign prisoners.

adversarial_corrections: single decisive specialist synthesis replayed; proposition remains within source wording and period

rows.bounded_proposition: Moon Pyramid archaeology securely demonstrates sacrificial killing and foreign-born sacrificial victims in earlier Teotihuacan construction phases. The reviewed packet does not establish slave status for those victims and does not establish a slavery/coercion practice specifically at the 500 CE anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not convert foreign origin, captivity, sacrifice, hierarchy or execution into slave status; do not project earlier Moon Pyramid sacrificial episodes forward to selected-year 500 CE or generalize them to citywide slavery prevalence.
rows.temporal_applicability: Earlier Teotihuacan sacrificial evidence is historical context only for the 500 CE target. No positive selected-year slavery applicability is established.
rows.temporal_precision: archaeological construction phases; key sacrificial interments precede the 500 CE anchor
rows.evidence_locus: Moon Pyramid sacrificial burials at Teotihuacan
rows.inference_extent: Earlier site-level coercive/sacrificial practice only; 500 CE slavery status/practice remains unknown in this packet
rows.language_access_limitations: English-language archaeological scholarship reviewed; no direct legal/status text identifies the victims as slaves.

normalized Spence/Pereira source to exact DOI

rows.bounded_proposition: Specialist synthesis of Songhay sources supports large-scale captive enslavement around the Gao-centered empire, including many captives brought to Gao after Askia Muhammad's 1498 Mossi campaign. Early-sixteenth-century eyewitness-derived material also describes slave sale and enslaved people at Gao. This supports a bounded Gao-level slavery/slave-market claim close to the 1500 anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not turn near-anchor 1498/early-sixteenth-century evidence into exact annual 1500 prevalence, and do not infer uniform slaveholding or one prevalence level across the whole Songhay Empire.
rows.temporal_applicability: Directly near anchor: 1498 captive influx; additional Gao observations from early sixteenth century. Treat 1500 as approximate/near-anchor, not exact annual observation.
rows.evidence_locus: Gao and Gao-centered Songhay court/market context
rows.inference_extent: Gao-level presence, captive influx and market/court slavery; no empire-wide prevalence estimate
rows.law_practice_note: Songhay Islamic legal restrictions on enslaving Muslims qualify acquisition practices but do not negate documented enslavement.
rows.network_territorial_note: Trans-Saharan movement is separate from Gao-local practice/market evidence.
rows.language_access_limitations: English-language specialist synthesis and translated early account reviewed; local chronicles/Arabic/Italian transmission not independently re-edited here.

adversarial_corrections: replaced unverified primary-source URL with verified 1896 Hakluyt Society edition record

rows.bounded_proposition: Shaolin is securely documented as an important medieval Buddhist monastery and as having received a substantial estate in the Sui period. Broader Chinese Buddhist institutions could use tenants, captive dependants and slaves, but the reviewed packet does not establish Shaolin-specific slave ownership or slave labour at the 1000 CE anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not infer Shaolin slaveholding at 1000 from an earlier estate grant, from generic Chinese Buddhist monastic labour patterns, or from slavery documented at other monasteries such as Dunhuang institutions.
rows.temporal_applicability: Target-specific Shaolin estate evidence is earlier than the 1000 CE anchor; generic monastic slavery evidence is contextual. No positive selected-year slavery applicability is established.
rows.temporal_precision: earlier institutional history plus broader medieval monastic context; exact 1000 labour regime unresolved
rows.evidence_locus: Shaolin estate for target-specific landholding; other Chinese Buddhist monasteries/Dunhuang for slavery context
rows.inference_extent: no Shaolin slavery claim at 1000 CE
rows.language_access_limitations: English-accessible scholarship reviewed; no target-specific Song-period Shaolin labour register or equivalent source located in the bounded packet.

sources.title: The Shaolin Monastery: History, Religion, and the Chinese Martial Arts

sources.title: Monuments in the Desert: A Note on Economic and Social Roots of the Development of Buddhism along the Silk Road
sources.author: Connie Chin
sources.notes: Shows broader monastery use of tenants/slaves and Dunhuang slave/property records; not Shaolin-specific.

adversarial_corrections: removed unsupported assumption that the earlier documented estate relation itself established the 1000 CE labour regime

rows.bounded_proposition: First-millennium Arabian epigraphy supports some enslavement, sale and captive/property relations in societies connected to trans-Arabian commerce, while Minaean inscriptions independently document traders using major caravan stopovers such as Ḥimā. The reviewed packet does not establish that enslaved people were themselves a documented commodity moving along the Incense Route around 100 BCE.
rows.required_abstention: Do not infer a slave-trading network from the conjunction of slavery in South Arabia and Minaean caravan commerce; do not paint the route or polities crossed by it as slave-trading territory.
rows.temporal_applicability: Evidence spans first-millennium BCE/CE Arabia and Minaean caravan activity; supports contextual possibility near 100 BCE but not a direct selected-year slave-traffic claim.
rows.evidence_locus: South Arabian/North Arabian epigraphic contexts and specific caravan nodes such as Ḥimā
rows.inference_extent: no route-wide slave-traffic claim; network relation remains unresolved
rows.network_territorial_note: Explicit network frame. Trade-route connectivity is not territorial practice, and slavery in connected societies is not evidence of slave movement along every corridor.
rows.language_access_limitations: Modern English specialist scholarship reviewed; ancient South/North Arabian epigraphy is interpreted through specialist publications rather than independently translated.

sources.title: Slavery in First Millennium Arabia: Epigraphy and the Qurʾān
sources.author: Valentina A. Grasso
sources.notes: Documents ambiguity of ʿbd while identifying captives and some purchase/sale/property evidence; explicitly warns against assuming widespread slavery.

sources.title: Minaeans at Ḥimā: The Epigraphic Corpus and Its Historical, Linguistic and Cultural Implications
sources.author: Alessia Prioletta; Mounir Arbach
sources.notes: Documents Minaean traders at a key trans-Arabian caravan stop; does not document slave traffic.

adversarial_corrections: confirmed that two separately supported facts—Arabian slavery and caravan connectivity—must not be joined into undocumented slave traffic

rows.bounded_proposition: Eighteenth-century evidence supports specific cases in which Inuit people in southern Labrador and west of Hudson Bay were captured, transferred or enslaved by colonial and neighboring Indigenous actors. This supports bounded external-enslavement/captive relations, but the reviewed packet does not establish a circumpolar Inuit institution of internal slavery or a territorial-practice state at the 1800 anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not generalize Labrador/Hudson Bay cases to all Inuit Arctic communities, do not infer internal Inuit slaveholding from Inuit people being enslaved by others, and do not project eighteenth-century episodes into exact selected-year 1800 continuity.
rows.temporal_applicability: Specific eighteenth-century episodes; no positive selected-year 1800 territorial-practice applicability established.
rows.evidence_locus: southern Labrador and west-of-Hudson-Bay interactions/fort contexts
rows.inference_extent: bounded external/captive relations for specific places and actors; circumpolar/internal territorial practice unknown
rows.network_territorial_note: Colonial/intercommunity captivity and transfer are external/network relations unless separate evidence supports internal territorial practice.
rows.language_access_limitations: English-language specialist scholarship reviewed; broad circumpolar and non-English/Indigenous-source coverage is incomplete.

sources.title: Slavery in New France: Resistance and Enslavement of Southern Labrador Inuit
sources.author: Greg Mitchell; Amanda Crompton
sources.notes: Directly studies enslaved Labrador Inuit and French Atlantic links.

sources.title: Trans-Indian Identity and the Inuit 'Other': Relations between the Chipewyan and Neighboring Aboriginal Communities in the Eighteenth Century
sources.author: Strother E. Roberts
sources.notes: Finds Inuit slaveholding by Cree/Chipewyan extremely rare and documents HBC-linked captive requests and 1774 Inuit slaves at Fort Prince of Wales.

rows.external_participation_summary: Specific external enslavement/captive relations are supported for southern Labrador and west-of-Hudson-Bay contexts.
rows.territorial_practice_summary: Internal/circumpolar Inuit slavery practice remains unestablished.
adversarial_corrections: separated externally imposed enslavement from internal territorial practice

rows.bounded_proposition: Specialist synthesis supports slavery as an important institution in Punic Carthage, including substantial slave labour in the agricultural hinterland and significant slave ownership among Carthaginian elites. This supports a bounded territorial-practice claim for Carthage around the Punic centuries containing the 500 BCE anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not infer a numeric enslaved share, universal slave-labour regime, uniform status across all Punic territories, or structural intensity beyond what the specialist synthesis supports.
rows.temporal_applicability: Punic Carthaginian institutional context spanning the relevant centuries; supports the 500 BCE anchor at period level.
rows.inference_extent: Carthage/hinterland institutional slavery; no quantitative empire-wide prevalence claim
rows.law_practice_note: The source treats legal position and economic role; legal/economic evidence is not converted into a population share.
rows.language_access_limitations: English-language specialist synthesis reviewed; underlying Punic and Graeco-Roman source corpus is accessed through the specialist analysis.

sources.title: Punic Carthage
sources.author: David M. Lewis
sources.notes: Dedicated specialist treatment of legal position/economic role of slaves in Punic Carthage.

adversarial_corrections: single decisive dedicated specialist chapter replayed; positive claim retained, quantitative/empire-wide inference remains prohibited

rows.bounded_proposition: The 1800 evidence securely establishes enslaved populations and slavery in multiple constituent Portuguese possessions, but the frozen source-native aggregate 'Portuguese Colonies' cannot receive one territorial-practice state. Constituent conditions vary too sharply for an empire-wide territorial classification.
rows.required_abstention: Do not average, color, rank, or narrate the dispersed Portuguese possessions as one slavery-practice territory. An empire-wide demographic total is an aggregate statistic, not the territorial historical condition of each possession.
rows.temporal_applicability: Constituent population evidence is centered on the 1800 cross-section; aggregate territorial applicability is intentionally undefined.
rows.temporal_precision: cross-sectional estimates around 1800; quality varies by territory
rows.evidence_locus: individual Portuguese overseas possessions represented in the 1800 demographic cross-section
rows.inference_extent: constituent-jurisdiction evidence only; no aggregate territorial practice inference
rows.law_practice_note: Resident enslaved-population estimates establish practice/presence at constituent level but do not by themselves resolve each jurisdiction's full legal regime.
rows.language_access_limitations: Portuguese/English-accessible demographic scholarship reviewed; underlying enumerations are heterogeneous and partly estimated.

rows.bounded_proposition: Mound 72 securely supports sacrificial killing, pronounced social differentiation and coercive elite power in an earlier Cahokia sequence. One published synthesis interprets some sacrificed individuals as slaves, while later bioarchaeological and mortuary reanalyses revise premises about origin, sex and ritual structure. The packet does not securely establish slave status and does not establish a slavery-practice state at the 1200 CE anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not infer slavery from execution, sacrifice, nutritional stress, social inferiority, presumed foreignness, captivity or elite coercive power alone; do not project the earlier Mound 72 evidence forward to selected-year 1200 or extrapolate it to citywide prevalence.
rows.temporal_applicability: Mound 72 evidence is principally earlier than the 1200 CE anchor and is retained as site-history context; no positive 1200 slavery applicability is established.
rows.temporal_precision: earlier Cahokia/Mound 72 mortuary sequence; not exact 1200
rows.inference_extent: earlier Mound 72 coercive/sacrificial evidence only; slave status and 1200 territorial practice remain unestablished
rows.language_access_limitations: English-language archaeological/bioarchaeological scholarship reviewed; no direct legal/status documentation exists.

rows.bounded_proposition: Slavery and slave trading were embedded in Fatimid Cairo and its ruling/military context, but the reviewed packet does not establish slave ownership, slave labour or a slavery institution specifically at al-Azhar around 1100 CE.
rows.required_abstention: Do not infer al-Azhar institutional slaveholding from slavery in Fatimid armies, Cairo households/markets, or from the enslaved/freed status of actors connected to the Fatimid conquest and foundation of Cairo.
rows.temporal_applicability: Fatimid Cairo context spans the 1100 anchor; al-Azhar-specific slavery remains unestablished.
rows.temporal_precision: period-level urban/imperial context; institution-specific status unresolved
rows.evidence_locus: Fatimid Cairo and broader Egyptian slave market/ruling context
rows.inference_extent: context only for al-Azhar; no institution-specific slavery claim
rows.network_territorial_note: Cairo-wide slave markets and military recruitment are contextual, not al-Azhar institutional practice.
rows.language_access_limitations: English-language specialist monograph reviewed; Geniza/Arabic source corpus not exhaustively reviewed for institution-specific al-Azhar ownership/labour.
